claims.text: The initial alloy is a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The constituent elements are homogeneously distributed in the initial alloy.
Composition can be systematically varied to increase atomic size mismatch while other relevant variables are controlled.
Increasing atomic size mismatch increases lattice distortion in single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced lattice distortion increases the energy barrier for dislocation motion.
Enhanced lattice distortion produces more effective dislocation pinning.
More effective dislocation pinning increases alloy hardness.
More effective dislocation pinning increases alloy strength.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have higher hardness than baseline alloys with lower mismatch.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have higher yield strength than baseline alloys with lower mismatch.
Baseline HEAs with minimal atomic size mismatch have lower lattice distortion.
Baseline HEAs with minimal atomic size mismatch have lower hardness and strength.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase HEAs without secondary-phase precipitation and with deformation dominated by dislocation motion.
The proposed relationship is expected under room-temperature, moderate-strain-rate conditions.
At high temperatures or when precipitates form, additional mechanisms may dominate the mechanical response.
The contributions of solid-solution strengthening and grain-boundary effects may vary with composition and processing.
Failure to observe a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase at greater mismatch would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe increased lattice distortion and dislocation pinning at greater mismatch would falsify the hypothesis.
